# rig-c — AI-Authored 2D Rigging and Animation, Verified Before It Is Written

One character painting goes in; a rigged, animated 2D character that plays in the browser or imports into the Spine 4.3 editor comes out. Every stage prints named, numeric findings and refuses by name what it cannot verify, so a file that fails a check never reaches the disk. A pass is a structural fact about the data, not a verdict on how the character looks.

**rig-c makes no images.** The painting and its layer split ([See-through](https://github.com/shitagaki-lab/see-through)) come from image models you run yourself — on your own GPU, or a free web demo. rig-c starts from those files, ships no model weights, and runs every one of its own steps on the CPU.

## From loose parts to a living rig

<figure class="figure-media">
  <div class="media">
    <video data-loop="the assembly demo" controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" poster="/assets/rigc-demo-poster.jpg" width="600" height="404" aria-label="Recorded video: fourteen drawn-from-scratch part PNGs converge into a character that breathes, blinks and waves — core's own film, with its authored animations compiled by rig-c">
      <source src="/assets/rigc-demo.mp4" type="video/mp4">
      <img src="/assets/rigc-demo-poster.jpg" alt="Fourteen drawn-from-scratch part PNGs converge into a character that breathes, blinks and waves" width="600" height="404">
    </video>
  </div>
  <figcaption><span class="media-kind">Recorded video</span> rig-c core's own film: fourteen parts drawn from scratch and three authored animations — <code>assemble</code>, <code>idle</code>, <code>wave</code> — compiled and rendered by rig-c; the filename labels and the caption band are the film's. From the <a href="https://github.com/rig-c/core">rig-c/core</a> README (film one).</figcaption>
</figure>

1. **[Parts](/docs/parts/)** merges the painting's two See-through layer sets into rig-space parts, then drafts bones, weighted meshes, physics and a looping idle.
2. **[Pose](/docs/pose/)** cleans a recorded body-18 pose sequence and retargets it onto the rig as an animation.
3. **[Core](/docs/core/)** compiles the rig and motion specs and gates them by named assertions — nothing is written unless every one passes.
4. **[Review](/docs/review/)** lets a person look at what an agent built and hand back feedback bound to a frame, bone or slot.
5. **[Play](/docs/play/)** and the **[adapters](/docs/adapters/)** run the compiled model in a page, PixiJS, Phaser or Three.js, with no Spine runtime.

Try it end to end with no GPU and no Python — about a minute of commands on an Apple M4: **[Getting started](/docs/getting-started/)**. See what agents do with it on the **[Exam](/exam/)**, and rebuild the published rigs from **[Examples](/examples/)**.

## The toolchain

| Package | Latest | Install | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [**@rig-c/parts**](/docs/parts/) | `1.41.0` | `npm i -D @rig-c/parts` | Assembles one character painting's decomposed See-through layers into rig-ready parts, then authors weighted meshes, bone chains, physics, and a looping idle over them. |
| [**@rig-c/pose**](/docs/pose/) | `0.35.0` | `npm i -D @rig-c/pose` | Cleans and retargets a body-18 pose sequence (from video, dataset, or hand-placed points) onto a rig that rig-c built, gated before keys are written. |
| [**rig-c / @rig-c/core**](/docs/core/) | `2.61.0` | `npm i -D rig-c` | The rig compiler: a rig spec and a motion spec in, Spine 4.3 skeleton data (`skeleton.json` + `.atlas`) and `skeleton.model.json` out — gated by named assertions before a byte is written (36 under the default `--profile spine`, all 50 under the opt-in `--profile rig-play`). |
| [**@rig-c/review**](/docs/review/) | `0.2.1` | `npm i -D @rig-c/review` | Local human inspection workspace: compare setup geometry, compiled-model playback, source video/sheets, and export frame/bone/slot-bound feedback ready to become an issue. |
| [**@rig-c/play**](/docs/play/) | `1.12.0` | `npm i @rig-c/play` | Plays `skeleton.model.json` in the browser with no Spine runtime — as plain DOM elements (`<img>` with CSS `matrix()`) or one `<canvas>` per player. |
| [**@rig-c/adapters**](/docs/adapters/) | `0.1.1` | `npm i @rig-c/pixi`<br>`npm i @rig-c/phaser`<br>`npm i @rig-c/three` | Plays a rig-c compiled model inside PixiJS 8, Phaser 4.2+, or Three.js 0.186+ through `@rig-c/play`'s posing core, with no Spine runtime. |

## Built for agents that cannot see

An AI agent asked to author a 2D rig cannot see the screen, and standard JSON parsers accept broken rigs in silence — a 4.2-shaped constraint vanishes in 4.3, a mismatched `size:` collapses every UV, a four-number curve array yields `NaN`, and a mesh whose vertex count equals its UV count silently loses its bone weights.

rig-c replaces that silence with five rules:

1. **The messages are the UI.** Every refusal names the object, the value found, and the value required. An agent reads one line and knows which field in which file to change — this is rig-c core's own example, a renamed page image:

   ```
   FAIL  A17_ATLAS_PAGE_FILES_EXIST: page "../images/hull.png" is not on disk at …/images/hull.png
   rigc: 1 assertion(s) failed
   ```

2. **Nothing is invented.** The compiler never guesses defaults from art or fills in missing numbers. Where the input is silent, it raises a named `CompileError`.
3. **Emit only after green — and green means structural.** `rigc build` writes to disk **only** if every named assertion of its profile passes: 36 under the default `spine` profile (*is this valid Spine 4.3 that any runtime plays correctly?*), all 50 under the opt-in `rig-play` profile. `rig-parts build` adds its own measured bars (seam, loop, folds and more) on top. None of this judges the picture: in rig-c core's words, *a rig with its head off its torso passes the gate*.
4. **What was not checked is printed too.** Every gate report names the profile that judged it and lists, on `PROF` lines, the rules that profile left out. `rig-parts check` names each bar that said `SKIP` and why, and a build accepted with failing bars (`compose --accept`) is, in its own words, for looking, not shipping.
5. **A person looks.** `rigc render` and `rigc inspect` draw what was built; [`@rig-c/review`](/docs/review/) puts it beside the source footage and exports feedback bound to a frame, bone or slot. The checks keep broken data off the disk; Review is where someone judges whether it looks right.

## Install

```sh
# Run the compiler CLI directly with Bun
bunx rig-c --help

# Install the authoring & compilation toolchain in a project
bun add -d @rig-c/parts rig-c @rig-c/pose @rig-c/review

# Install the zero-Spine-runtime browser player
bun add @rig-c/play
```

### Install Agent Skills

`rig-c` and `@rig-c/parts` ship [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) (`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, inside each npm package) that route coding agents directly to the authoritative authoring rules:

```sh
# Codex, Gemini CLI, or Antigravity: link rig-c's skills into .agents/skills/
bun add -d rig-c
bun rigc skills install

# Claude Code: the rig-c/core repository is a plugin marketplace
/plugin marketplace add rig-c/core
/plugin install rigc@rigc
```

## Package names and aliases

- `rig-c`, `@rig-c/core`, and `spine-rigc` are the same compiler package on npm and install the `rigc` command.
- `@rig-c/parts`, `rig-parts`, and `spine-parts` are the same part-assembly package and install the `rig-parts` command.
- `@rig-c/play`, `rig-play`, and `spine-html` are the same browser player package.

## Licensing, stated plainly

rig-c's code is **MIT**. Which Spine terms apply depends on what plays the output, because `rigc` writes both Spine 4.3 skeleton data and rig-c's own model (`skeleton.model.json`):

- **rig-c's model in [`@rig-c/play`](/docs/play/) or an [engine adapter](/docs/adapters/)**: these link nothing from Esoteric Software and integrate no Spine Runtime.
- **Spine data in an official Spine Runtime or the Spine Web Player**: the [Spine Runtimes License](https://esotericsoftware.com/spine-runtimes-license) applies to that integration.
- **Spine data in the Spine editor**: the [Spine Editor License Agreement](https://esotericsoftware.com/spine-editor-license) applies.

Sample paintings and layers carry their own licences — Getting Started's example inputs are CC BY-NC 4.0. The full table, with sources: **[Licensing](/docs/licensing/)**.

# Docs

rig-c is a set of small packages that hand files to each other: a painting split into layers goes in at one end, and a rig that plays in a browser, a game engine, or the Spine editor comes out at the other. These pages explain what each package is for and how it works. Flags, schemas, and every rule live in the package's own repository — each page links there.

## Start here

- [**Getting Started**](/docs/getting-started/): Tested 10-step no-GPU, no-Python walkthrough (about a minute of commands on an Apple M4) from pre-decomposed character layers to a compiled rig with idle and wave animations playing in the browser, plus downstream export routes.
- [**Parts**](/docs/parts/) — `@rig-c/parts`: @rig-c/parts is a Bun CLI that turns one character painting and its See-through layer decomposition into measured parts, a rig-c rig spec and an idle, gated and packed by rig-c into Spine 4.3 skeleton data.
- [**Pose**](/docs/pose/) — `@rig-c/pose`: @rig-c/pose is a Bun CLI that cleans a body-18 joint-position sequence and retargets it onto a rig-c rig as gated, verified bone keys.
- [**Core**](/docs/core/) — `rig-c`: rig-c (also @rig-c/core, CLI rigc) compiles a JSON rig spec and motion spec plus loose part PNGs into Spine 4.3 skeleton data, gated by named assertions so nothing invalid is written.
- [**Review**](/docs/review/) — `@rig-c/review`: @rig-c/review is a local, loopback-only CLI and browser workspace for a person to inspect a compiled rig, compare it with reference video, and save structured, source-bound feedback for the producing agent.
- [**Play**](/docs/play/) — `@rig-c/play`: @rig-c/play is the browser runtime that loads rigc's compiled skeleton.model.json and plays it as plain DOM elements (CSS matrix per rigid slot, small canvases per mesh) or as one canvas per player.
- [**Adapters**](/docs/adapters/) — `@rig-c/pixi, @rig-c/phaser, @rig-c/three`: @rig-c/pixi, @rig-c/phaser and @rig-c/three play rigc's skeleton.model.json inside PixiJS, Phaser or Three.js scenes, posed through @rig-c/play and drawn with each host's native objects, without a Spine runtime.
- [**Licensing**](/docs/licensing/): Licensing by path: rig-c code is MIT; rig-c's own model played by @rig-c/play or the adapters integrates no Spine Runtime; Spine data in a Spine Runtime or the Spine Editor falls under Esoteric Software's terms; sample assets carry their own licences (Getting Started's inputs are CC BY-NC 4.0).

## How the pieces fit

1. **Parts** turns the painting's layers into rig-space parts and authors a first rig over them.
2. **Pose** turns a recorded body pose sequence into an animation on that rig.
3. **Core** (`rigc`) compiles the rig and motion specs, gates them by named assertions, and writes only when every one passes.
4. **Review** lets a person look at what an agent built and hand back feedback bound to a frame, bone, or slot.
5. **Play** and the **adapters** run the compiled model in a page or a game engine with no Spine runtime.

================================================================================
URL: https://rig-c.org/docs/getting-started/
Markdown: https://rig-c.org/docs/getting-started/index.md
Repository: https://github.com/rig-c/getting-started
================================================================================

# Getting Started with rig-c

You start with one painting of a character. You end with that character rigged — split into movable pieces on a skeleton — breathing, blinking, and waving in your browser.

Repository: <https://github.com/rig-c/getting-started>

## The whole pipeline in three steps

1. **Paint one character.** Any image model or illustration workflow produces a front-facing, full-body character PNG on a plain white background with arms clear of the body.
2. **Split it into layers, and mark the joints.** [See-through](https://github.com/shitagaki-lab/see-through) cuts the painting into layered parts (twice: full figure + head crop). Body-18 joints come from a lightweight CPU script (`rtmlib`) or hand placement.
3. **Run the rig-c packages on the CPU.** `@rig-c/parts`, `rig-c`, `@rig-c/pose`, and `@rig-c/play` assemble the parts, author meshes and bones, gate the build, retarget motion, and play it in the browser. **No GPU is used in step 3.**

## Try it first — no GPU, no Python

This builds a published example character whose painting and See-through layers are already made, then plays it in your browser. The joints come from a hand-placed file that ships with the guide, so the only tools you need are [Bun](https://bun.sh) 1.2 or later, `git` and `curl`, on macOS or Linux (Windows is not tested).

**How long it takes.** Every command below was run as written, in order, from an empty folder on 2026-10-19 — Apple M4, Bun 1.4.2, and whatever `bun add` resolved that day (`rig-c` 2.61.0, `@rig-c/parts` 1.41.0, `@rig-c/pose` 0.35.0, `@rig-c/play` 1.12.0):

| Run | Steps 1–10 |
| --- | --- |
| Empty Bun cache (includes downloading the packages and the 41 MB example) | 56 s |
| A second run, caches warm | 62 s |

Steps 5 (assemble) and 8 (build) are most of it. A slower machine or network takes longer; the two runs above are the only measurements.

### 1. Install the packages

```sh
mkdir rig-c-start && cd rig-c-start
git clone https://github.com/rig-c/getting-started
mkdir my-rig && cd my-rig
bun add @rig-c/parts rig-c @rig-c/pose @rig-c/play
```

Every command from here on runs in `my-rig`.

### 2. Get the example inputs

```sh
curl -L -o exam.tar.gz https://codeload.github.com/rig-c/exam/tar.gz/01436ee3f02c189fe1a1e9656fe62068889837f5
tar -xzf exam.tar.gz --strip-components=3 exam-01436ee3f02c189fe1a1e9656fe62068889837f5/tasks/01-build/inputs
tar -xzf exam.tar.gz --strip-components=1 exam-01436ee3f02c189fe1a1e9656fe62068889837f5/LICENSE exam-01436ee3f02c189fe1a1e9656fe62068889837f5/NOTICE.md
rm exam.tar.gz
```

You now have `inputs/` with `painting.png`, `layers/full/` and `layers/head/`. These inputs are **CC BY-NC 4.0** — see [Licensing](/docs/licensing/).

### 3. Start the config

```sh
cat > config.json <<'EOF'
{
  "key": "exam-01",
  "seethrough": { "resolution": 1024, "steps": 30, "seed": 42, "offload": true },
  "assemble": { "rig_scale": 0.5 }
}
EOF
bunx rig-parts inputs --source inputs/painting.png --config config.json --out work
```

You should see `st_input_full.png 2432x2432` and a note that there is no head box yet.

### 4. Find the head box

```sh
bunx rig-parts layers inputs/layers/full
bunx rig-parts propose --head-box --full inputs/layers/full --canvas 1664x2432 | tail -n 1 > work/head_box.json
bun ../getting-started/scripts/take.ts work/head_box.json config.json seethrough.head_box=head_box
bunx rig-parts inputs --source inputs/painting.png --config config.json --out work
```

You should see `29 layer(s): 29 with opaque pixels`, `0 WARN line(s)`, `work/head_box.json` holding `{"head_box":[616,32,1132,548]}`, then `st_input_head.png 516x516`.

### 5. Assemble the parts

```sh
bunx rig-parts assemble --propose-plan --source inputs/painting.png --full inputs/layers/full --head inputs/layers/head --config config.json > work/plan.json
bun ../getting-started/scripts/take.ts work/plan.json config.json assemble.plan=plan assemble.extend_below_crop=extend_below_crop
bunx rig-parts assemble --source inputs/painting.png --full inputs/layers/full --head inputs/layers/head --config config.json --out work
```

You should see `22 part(s) on a 832x1216 rig`, then `recomposite vs source: mean |d|=1.13, within 8: 97.8%`.

### 6. Put the joints in place

~~~sh
sed -n '/^```json$/,/^```$/p' ../getting-started/docs/KEYPOINTS.md | sed '1d;$d' > keypoints.json
~~~

This copies the hand-placed body-18 joints for this painting out of the guide's [`docs/KEYPOINTS.md`](https://github.com/rig-c/getting-started/blob/main/docs/KEYPOINTS.md), which also explains how to place them for a painting of your own.

**Detecting the joints with a script instead** needs [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and downloads about 300 MB of pose models on first run:

```sh
uv run --with rtmlib --with onnxruntime python ../getting-started/scripts/keypoints.py inputs/painting.png --out keypoints.json
```

With this painting the script puts the left ankle just off the shoe art. On `@rig-c/parts` 1.41.1, step 7 then prints one `LINT` beginning `LINT foot_l at [428, 1077], the l_ankle joint and leg_l1's tip, lies on none of leg_l's art within 1 px along its joint line`, drafts that leg without its ankle cut, and the build goes green (measured 2026-10-20 from empty caches: all ten steps in 166 s, the model download included). From 1.17.0 through 1.41.0 the same joints made step 8 refuse with `ASSEMBLE_LIMB_JOINT_ON_ART`; use the hand-placed file if you are on one of those.

### 7. Draft the bones

```sh
bunx rig-parts propose --parts work/rig --source inputs/painting.png --out work --keypoints keypoints.json
bun ../getting-started/scripts/take.ts work/proposal.json config.json bones meshes regions motion limbs
```

You should see a coverage line starting `coverage: 42 bone(s) — 29 checked and clean`. This is where a person would correct the draft; the example uses it as is.

### 8. Build the rig

```sh
bunx rig-parts build --config config.json --source inputs/painting.png --full inputs/layers/full --head inputs/layers/head --out out --loop
```

You should see `check: PASS; 11 of 12 bar(s) measured, 1 skipped (STRESS_OFF_CHAIN)`, then `build: PASS`. Open `out/idle.gif`: the character breathes and blinks in a loop.

<figure>
  <div class="media">
    <video data-loop="the idle" controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" poster="/assets/docs/getting-started-idle-poster.jpg" width="316" height="640" aria-label="Recorded video: the example character standing, breathing and blinking once in her idle loop">
      <source src="/assets/docs/getting-started-idle.mp4" type="video/mp4">
      <img src="/assets/docs/getting-started-idle-poster.jpg" alt="The example character standing at rest" width="316" height="640">
    </video>
  </div>
  <figcaption><span class="media-kind">Recorded video</span> The idle this walkthrough wrote, unedited: 40 frames at 12 fps from <code>out/idle.png</code>, the lossless copy <code>build --loop</code> writes beside <code>out/idle.gif</code>. Made by the commands above, run as written on 2026-10-20 with <code>@rig-c/parts</code> 1.42.0 and <code>rig-c</code> 2.64.1.</figcaption>
</figure>

A skipped bar is named with its reason; any `FAIL` line means nothing was written, and the line says what to change. A green build means the checks passed — whether it looks right is yours to judge (`out/idle.gif`, or [Review](/docs/review/)).

### 9. Give it a wave

```sh
bun ../getting-started/scripts/wave.ts keypoints.json wave.pose.json
bunx rig-pose clean --pose wave.pose.json --out wave.pose.clean.json
cat > map.json <<'EOF'
{
  "spec": "rig-pose-map/1",
  "chains": [
    { "name": "trunk", "bones": ["chest"], "joints": ["mid_hip", "neck"], "aim": ["neck"] },
    { "name": "arm_r", "bones": ["sleeve_r0", "sleeve_r1"], "joints": ["r_shoulder", "r_elbow", "r_wrist"], "bend": "free" },
    { "name": "arm_l", "bones": ["sleeve_l0", "sleeve_l1"], "joints": ["l_shoulder", "l_elbow", "l_wrist"], "bend": "free" }
  ],
  "translate": { "bone": "hip", "joint": "mid_hip", "scale": { "pose": ["mid_hip", "neck"], "rig": ["hip", "neck"] } }
}
EOF
bunx rig-pose retarget --rig out/rig --map map.json --pose wave.pose.clean.json --out wave.motion.json --name wave --profile spine-html --build wave-build
```

You should see `wave.ts: 73 frame(s), 3 s at 24 fps`, a `GATE … green` line, and `wrote wave.motion.json — animations: idle, wave`. `wave-build/` holds the rig with both animations.

### 10. Play it in your browser

```sh
bun ../getting-started/scripts/serve.ts
```

Open <http://localhost:3000/?model=wave-build/skeleton.model.json&anim=wave>: the character raises her right arm and waves; the menu switches to `idle`. Ctrl+C stops the server.

<figure>
  <div class="media">
    <video data-loop="the wave" controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" poster="/assets/docs/getting-started-wave-poster.jpg" width="388" height="640" aria-label="Recorded video: the example character raises her right arm above her head, waves, and lowers it back to rest">
      <source src="/assets/docs/getting-started-wave.mp4" type="video/mp4">
      <img src="/assets/docs/getting-started-wave-poster.jpg" alt="The example character standing at rest before the wave" width="388" height="640">
    </video>
  </div>
  <figcaption><span class="media-kind">Recorded video</span> The <code>wave</code> animation in this walkthrough's <code>wave-build/</code>, unedited: 73 frames, 3 s at 24 fps, from rest back to rest. Drawn frame by frame by rig-c's own poser (<code>bunx rigc render --candidate wave-build --animation wave --fps 24 --max 640 --poser core</code>) rather than filmed from the browser player. Same run as the idle above: <code>@rig-c/parts</code> 1.42.0, <code>rig-c</code> 2.64.1, <code>@rig-c/pose</code> 0.36.0.</figcaption>
</figure>

The full guide — making your own character, the GPU routes, troubleshooting and every measured figure — is the [rig-c/getting-started README](https://github.com/rig-c/getting-started#readme) and its [docs/REFERENCE.md](https://github.com/rig-c/getting-started/blob/main/docs/REFERENCE.md).

## Three ways to use the output

1. **On the web with [`@rig-c/play`](/docs/play/) or [`@rig-c/adapters`](/docs/adapters/)**: Load `skeleton.model.json` and part PNGs directly. The packages are MIT and integrate no Spine Runtime.
2. **In the Spine 4.3 Editor**: Import `out/check/build/skeleton.json` via `Import Data` and point `Images` to `out/rig/images/` to refine timelines by hand (requires rig-c 2.51.1+; the editor is under the Spine Editor License Agreement).
3. **In a game engine via official Spine Runtimes**: Load `skeleton.json` and `skeleton.atlas` in Unity, Godot, Unreal, or C++ runtimes under the Spine Runtimes License.

The example inputs in step 2 come from [rig-c/exam](https://github.com/rig-c/exam) and are **CC BY-NC 4.0**, not MIT: free to use with credit, not for commercial use, and what you build from them carries that licence. Which terms each route brings: [Licensing](/docs/licensing/).

# @rig-c/parts

<p class="mod-role">One painting and its See-through layers in — measured parts, a drafted rig and a looping idle out.</p>

<figure class="mod-hero">
  <div class="media">
    <video data-loop="the parts loop" controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" poster="/assets/docs/parts-explode-poster.jpg" width="1280" height="720" aria-label="Recorded video: Character 1 assembled from her seventeen parts, dissolving into a labelled grid of those parts and back">
      <source src="/assets/docs/parts-explode.mp4" type="video/mp4">
      <img src="/assets/docs/parts-explode-poster.jpg" alt="Character 1 assembled from her seventeen parts" width="1280" height="720">
    </video>
  </div>
  <figcaption><span class="media-kind">Recorded video</span> Character 1's 17 parts from <code>out/parts/</code>. The assembled figure that opens and closes the loop is drawn at the positions <code>parts.json</code> records, in the rig's draw order; the labelled grid and the dissolves between them are this page's illustration.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p class="mod-skip">Skip to <a href="#install">Install</a> · <a href="#inputs-and-outputs">Inputs and outputs</a> · <a href="#limits">Limits</a> · <a href="#go-deeper">Docs</a></p>

*This page follows Character 1 from the Family set: here it is split into parts. Every module works on its own; this order is one path, not a requirement.*

Cutting a painted character into rig parts is slow, and the mistakes show up late: a layer holds the wrong pixels, a part leaves a hole, a chain swings a skirt about its middle. `rig-parts` measures each of these and prints the number, so an agent that cannot see the image can still tell where it went wrong. A refusal names the object, the value found and the value required; nothing is written after a red, and no value is invented where the input is silent.

## How Character 1 was made

### 1. Two See-through runs

<figure class="figure-wide">
  <img src="/assets/docs/parts-layers.jpg" alt="A sheet of every See-through layer of Character 1, each labelled with its tag, size and opaque pixel count" width="1400" height="1225" loading="lazy">
  <figcaption>The layers See-through returned — one run on the full figure, one on a square crop around the head, because a full-figure run leaves the eyes too small to separate. Each tile is labelled with its tag, size and opaque pixels.</figcaption>
</figure>

### 2. Parts, and what they miss

`assemble` merges the two runs into rig-space parts, then lays them back together and compares the result with the painting. The error map is the point of that step: it shows, in colour, the painting that no part holds.

<div class="compare cols-3">
  <figure><img src="/assets/docs/parts-painting.jpg" alt="Character 1's painting" width="315" height="900" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The painting</figcaption></figure>
  <figure><img src="/assets/docs/parts-recomposite.jpg" alt="The 17 parts laid back together" width="315" height="900" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The 17 parts, recomposited</figcaption></figure>
  <figure><img src="/assets/docs/parts-errormap.jpg" alt="Error map: the figure in grey with thin red and blue edges where the parts and the painting differ" width="315" height="900" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The error map</figcaption></figure>
</div>

<div class="compare">
  <figure><img src="/assets/docs/parts-painting-zoom.jpg" alt="Close-up of the painting: Character 1's left hand resting on her forearm" width="660" height="660" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The painting, around the resting hand</figcaption></figure>
  <figure><img src="/assets/docs/parts-errormap-zoom.jpg" alt="The same close-up on the error map: a thin red line along the hand and sleeve edge, with a few blue pixels" width="660" height="660" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The error map there: <strong>red</strong> is painting no part holds, <strong>blue</strong> is a part whose colour is more than 40 off</figcaption></figure>
</div>

For this build `parts.json` records a mean difference of 0.873 per pixel, 98.3% of pixels within 8, and 6,041 uncovered error pixels. The largest hole it lists is 834 px along the edge of `bottomwear`. A clean recomposite is what lets the rig move without showing the background through.

### 3. A drafted rig that idles

`propose` drafts bones, weighted meshes, regions and a looping idle over those parts, for a person or an agent to correct; `build` runs assemble, rig and check in one process and stops at the first refusal.

<div class="compare">
  <figure>
    <div class="media">
      <video data-loop="the idle" controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" poster="/assets/docs/parts-idle-poster.jpg" width="246" height="640" aria-label="Recorded video: Character 1 breathing in its idle loop">
        <source src="/assets/docs/parts-idle.mp4" type="video/mp4">
        <img src="/assets/docs/parts-idle-poster.jpg" alt="Character 1 standing" width="246" height="640">
      </video>
    </div>
    <figcaption><span class="media-kind">Recorded video</span> The idle, as <code>build --loop</code> wrote it: 41 frames at 12 fps.</figcaption>
  </figure>
  <figure><img src="/assets/docs/parts-contact.jpg" alt="A contact sheet of the idle's 41 frames" width="401" height="775" loading="lazy"><figcaption><code>check</code>'s contact sheet of the same idle — what the measured bars read.</figcaption></figure>
</div>

The idle then goes on: [Pose](/docs/pose/) gives the same rig a recorded motion, and [Core](/docs/core/) is the compiler every one of these builds went through.

## How it works

1. **Inputs.** `inputs` cuts the two images See-through is fed: the painting on a white square, and a square crop around the head.
2. **Layers.** You run See-through by any route — a hosted demo, the upstream CLI, or ComfyUI. rig-parts reads its `.psd` or the ComfyUI wrapper form; an artist's own layered PSD works too, with no See-through step.
3. **Assemble.** The two runs merge into rig-space parts; uncovered holes are listed and the error map shows them.
4. **Propose.** Bones, meshes, regions and an idle are drafted with an overlay to correct against. It is a draft, not a step of `build`: you copy its sections into `config.json`, and LINT lines flag what still looks wrong.
5. **Build.** Assemble, rig and check in one process; compiling, gating and packing are rig-c's.

**Key terms.** *See-through layers* — the painting's decomposition, one run on the full figure and one on the head. *Parts* — the merged, measured pieces in rig space (`parts.json`). *Proposal* — the drafted bones, meshes, regions and motion, to be corrected. *Config* — `config.json`, the character's part plan, head box, bones and idle; unknown or missing fields are refused by name. *FAIL line* — a refusal that names a rule and ends with `(see rig-parts guide <RULE>)`.

## Install

```sh
npm i -D @rig-c/parts
rig-parts --help
```

Requires [Bun](https://bun.sh) 1.2 or later; rig-c comes with it as a dependency. Which Spine terms apply depends on what plays the output: see [Licensing](/docs/licensing/).

## Inputs and outputs

| In | Out |
| --- | --- |
| One character painting (`painting.png`) | `check/build/skeleton.json`, `skeleton.atlas`, `skeleton.png` — Spine 4.3 data and one packed page |
| Two See-through layer sets (`full`, `head`), as the ComfyUI wrapper form or a `.psd` | `parts/*.png`, `parts.json`, the recomposite and its error map |
| A character config (`config.json`) | `rig/rig.json`, `rig/motion.json` in rig-c's spec |
| Optional body-18 keypoints for `propose --keypoints` | `check/`: both gate files, the idle's frames, `contact.png`, `check.json`; with `--loop`, the idle as APNG and GIF |

## Limits

From the README's own *What it does not do*:

- **One depth value per layer.** A layer that is in front of another in one place and behind it in another is right in the still and wrong once it moves.
- **No expression or lip-sync, and no jiggle.** The mouth is one layer; nothing here proposes, keys or judges a soft region.
- **Occluded pixels are See-through's synthesis**, not the artist's.
- **No success rate is claimed** — ten characters measured stage by stage is an existence proof, not a rate.
- **No WebP**: `loop` writes GIF and APNG.
- **The proposer reads tags, not pictures**, and reads the torso by screen y unless it is given keypoints; it does not estimate a pose itself.

- [README: The loop, for an agent](https://github.com/rig-c/parts#the-loop-for-an-agent), the full command sequence
- [README: What it does not do](https://github.com/rig-c/parts#what-it-does-not-do)

# @rig-c/pose

<p class="mod-role">Joint positions over time in — bone keys on a rig-c rig out, checked before they are written.</p>

<figure class="mod-hero">
  <div class="media">
    <video data-loop="the swing comparison" controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" poster="/assets/docs/pose-swing-poster.jpg" width="806" height="792" aria-label="Recorded video: on the left a stick-figure pose swinging its right forearm; in the middle Character 1 swinging her coffee cup the same way, a few degrees each side, twice in three seconds; on the right an inset of her forearm and cup at twice the size, where the swing is easier to see">
      <source src="/assets/docs/pose-swing.mp4" type="video/mp4">
      <img src="/assets/docs/pose-swing-poster.jpg" alt="Side by side: the source pose's hanging arm, Character 1 holding her cup at rest, and an inset of her forearm and cup at twice the size" width="806" height="792">
    </video>
  </div>
  <figcaption><span class="media-kind">Recorded video</span> Left: the source — 18 body joints at 24 fps, the right forearm swinging the cup like a pendulum about the elbow. Middle: Character 1's rig playing the motion <code>rig-pose retarget</code> wrote from it, drawn by <code>rigc render</code>; inset: forearm and cup at 2×. The swing is deliberately small — a sine of ±4° centred 2.5° toward her body, for reasons <a href="#a-motion-that-fits-the-rig">below</a>. The clip is the whole motion, two swings in 3 s, and loops where the motion does.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p class="mod-skip">Skip to <a href="#install">Install</a> · <a href="#inputs-and-outputs">Inputs and outputs</a> · <a href="#limits">Limits</a> · <a href="#go-deeper">Docs</a></p>

*This page follows Character 1 from the Family set: here it is given a motion. Every module works on its own; this order is one path, not a requirement.*

A pose model reads each frame alone, so joints shake from frame to frame, and every key would carry that shake. Mapping picture angles onto bones has traps of its own: setup rotations, and parents that turn their children. `rig-pose` cleans the sequence once, where it can be inspected, then turns each mapped bone to point along its segment — and refuses to write keys that do not land where the pose asked.

## How the swing reached Character 1

### A motion that fits the rig

The first try was a full arm-over-the-head wave. It passed every check — the gate, the landing tolerance, the fold test — and the render still showed the sleeve torn open at the shoulder once the arm went overhead. A pass is structural, so the motion has to suit the character and the rig: here, the coffee cup she is already holding, swung loosely like a pendulum from the elbow, written as two swings in three seconds: the forearm follows a sine with a 1.5 s period, eased at both ends, and the sequence was cleaned with <code>--loop</code>, so the motion returns to its first frame at 3 s and the hero clip above is all of it.

Getting that right took measuring rather than looking. Swung outward, the arm uncovered the edge of the trousers it hides in the painting, which See-through had to synthesize; swung inward, it slid under the shirt, because the arm part is drawn beneath `topwear`. And the hand-placed joints did not sit exactly on the rig's bones, so even "at rest" the retarget turned the upper arm 4.5° and the chest 2.6° away from how the rig was drawn. So the rest pose was aligned first — every track reads 0 at rest — and then the arm part was rendered alone and with the whole rig, counting, frame by frame, how many of its pixels end up covered by another part:

| Animation | Arm pixels covered (rim excluded), worst frame |
| --- | --- |
| `idle`, as the rig was drawn | 926 |
| the first swing (upper arm and forearm, rest not aligned) | 1,854 |
| the previous swing (forearm only, aligned rest, outward half cut) | 1,242 |
| this swing (sine ±4° centred 2.5° in) | 1,295 |

What the extra ~370 px are: a thin strip along the inside edge of the sleeve, where its mesh meets the shirt. The sleeve and cuff stay in front.

The outward side got the same treatment. Counting pixels on the body side of the resting arm that turn into bare background — a hole in the trousers behind it — a ±6° swing opened up to 5,173 px at its outermost frame. The previous swing cut its outward half to 30% of the inward one (worst frame 1,124 px), which kept the trousers whole but made the swing a twitch. This one is a whole sine, centred toward the body instead: its worst frame opens 1,476 px, under the 1,500 px set before measuring (the breathing `idle` alone opens 1,138). Most of that count is the gap between forearm and leg widening, which is what a swing should do; the tear itself is a notch in the trouser edge just below the cuff, where See-through synthesized cloth the painting never showed. Swung symmetrically about the rest pose, the notch shows from ±4° (5,045 px at ±5°, 4,184 at ±4°, 3,117 at ±3°), so the swing is centred where the rig can take it. A wider swing about the rest pose waits on the rig: an arm cut free of the torso and a trouser edge that holds.

<figure>
  <img src="/assets/docs/pose-swing-tear.jpg" alt="Three close-ups of Character 1's forearm and the trouser edge beside it at twice the size: at rest; swung 4 degrees outward from rest, with a jagged notch in the trouser edge below the cuff; and at this swing's outermost frame, with the edge whole" width="804" height="720" loading="lazy">
  <figcaption>At twice the size: the rest pose; a symmetric ±4° swing at its outermost, where the synthesized trouser edge below the cuff tears; this swing at its outermost (−1.5°), where it holds.</figcaption>
</figure>

The map names two chains: the **trunk** (hip to neck) on the `chest` bone, and the **right arm** (shoulder, elbow, wrist) on the two sleeve bones. The rig has no left-arm bones (no `sleeve_l` in its `rig.json`), so that arm stays as painted, and the hand with the cup is not mapped: it turns with the forearm.

| Track the rig received | From the pose | Range over the loop |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sleeve_r0` rotate | shoulder → elbow | 0° (held) |
| `sleeve_r1` rotate | elbow → wrist | −1.49° (outward) to 6.49° (inward), a sine |
| `chest` rotate | hip → neck | 0° (held) |
| `hip` translate | hip | 0, 0 (held) |

**Direction, not length.** Each bone points the way its segment points in the picture but keeps the rig's own length (upper arm 300 px in the pose, 267 units on the rig; forearm 335 px and 303 units).

<div class="compare">
  <figure><img src="/assets/docs/pose-keypoints.jpg" alt="Character 1's painting with 18 labelled body joints drawn over it" width="400" height="1142" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Where the motion starts: 18 body joints placed by hand on the painting (joints under the clothes marked occluded).</figcaption></figure>
  <figure><img src="/assets/docs/pose-swing-ends.jpg" alt="Two side-by-side frames: the swing at its outermost and its innermost, source pose and rig each" width="1220" height="792" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The two ends of the swing (t = 0.54 s and 1.29 s). Orange is what the map carries; the rest of the skeleton has no bone to go to.</figcaption></figure>
</div>

### What it checked before writing

```
rig-pose retarget: 73 frame(s), 3.000s — 4 track(s); min-score 0.3, flip off, short off, bends refuse (tolerance 0°)
  GATE   rigc build --profile spine-html: green — 52 assertions: 26 measured (26 passed, 0 failed), 26 skipped, 0 not in profile "rig-play"
  LAND   bone "sleeve_r0" aim — worst |reached − asked| 0.0000764° at frame 0 (t=0.000s); the tolerance is 0.01°
  LAND   bone "sleeve_r1" aim — worst |reached − asked| 0.000559° at frame 0 (t=0.000s); the tolerance is 0.01°
  FOLD   rigc render --folds at 24 fps: no mesh folds
  wrote swing.motion.json — animations: idle, swing
```

The rig is built with the new animation and gated before anything is written; every mapped bone, posed by rig-c's own poser, has to land within 0.01° of what the pose asked on every frame. The run also says what it left out: 26 `IDLE-DROPPED` lines name the breathing and hair tracks that were not carried into `swing` — which is why only the arm moves. And then someone still has to look: the torn first try passed all of these lines.

The joints were placed by hand on the painting (the way the getting-started guide's `docs/KEYPOINTS.md` describes); the swing is a three-second test motion made from them, not footage. Next, [Core](/docs/core/) is the compiler that gated this build, [Review](/docs/review/) is where a person checks a motion against footage, and [Play](/docs/play/) runs this one live.

## How it works

1. **Clean.** `rig-pose clean` removes spikes, fills low-score or occluded joints from their neighbours, smooths each joint and holds joints that have stopped. `retarget` reads only a sequence `clean` wrote; COCO-17 input is converted with `--coco`.
2. **Map.** You write which bones carry which joints, chain by chain.
3. **Retarget.** For every frame and every mapped bone, the bone is turned so it points the way its segment points, minus its setup angle and its parent's turn.
4. **Check.** The gate must be green with and without the animation, every mapped bone must land on its angle, hinges must bend one way; otherwise nothing is written and every reason is printed.
5. **Say what it cannot decide.** Lines such as `HOLD`, `END-ON` and `IDLE-DROPPED` name what to look at.

**Key terms.** *body-18* — the 18 joints the sequence uses; `r`/`l` are the subject's sides. *Chain* — a limb in the map, as bones that descend from one another. *Lands* — a mapped bone within 0.01° of the angle the pose asks for. *Cleaned record* — the block `clean` writes into the sequence, which `retarget` requires.

## Install

```sh
npm i -D @rig-c/pose
bunx rig-pose retarget --rig out/rig --map map.json --pose swing.pose.clean.json --out swing.motion.json --name swing --build swing-build
```

Needs [Bun](https://bun.sh) 1.2 or later on `PATH`; rig-c comes as a dependency.

## Inputs and outputs
| In | Out |
| --- | --- |
| A body-18 pose sequence, `rig-pose-sequence/1` (COCO-17 with `--coco`) | A cleaned sequence carrying its `cleaned` record (`rig-pose clean`) |
| A rig built with rig-c: the `rig/` directory with `rig.json` and `motion.json` | A motion spec (`--out`, e.g. `motion.json`) with the bone keys |
| A map, `rig-pose-map/1` — which bones carry which joints | A JSON report, `rig-pose-report/1` (`--report`), and a gated build (`--build`) |
| For `compare`: a reference and a render sequence on one time base | `compare.json` and a `compare.png` sheet, differences per body unit, worst first |

## Limits
- **"0.x is the prototype."** The format, the command and the output can change in any release until 1.0 (README, intro).
- **Does not extract poses from video**: the input is joint positions, from a pose model, a dataset or by hand (README §"What it does not do").
- **2D only — does not turn the body**: a segment pointing at the camera foreshortens and "the rig cannot"; the direction is matched, not the length (README §"What it does not do").
- **No front/behind order per segment, no blinks or mouth shapes**, and cloth physics is not fitted to the reference (README §"What it does not do").
- **No hands or fingers** — there are no bones for them yet (README §"What it does not do").
- No importable API: the supported surface is the `rig-pose` command (README §"Requirements").

- [What it does](https://github.com/rig-c/pose#what-it-does)
- [The pose: `rig-pose-sequence/1`](https://github.com/rig-c/pose#the-pose-rig-pose-sequence1)

# rig-c core (`rigc`)

<p class="mod-role">The compiler: a rig spec and a motion spec in, Spine 4.3 skeleton data out — and nothing written unless every named check passes.</p>

<div class="triptych" role="group" aria-label="One mistake, its refusal, and the fix">
<figure><figcaption><span class="label fail">1 · The mistake</span> one weight on one neck vertex</figcaption>
<pre><code class="language-diff">                 "bone": "chest",
                 "x": -112,
                 "y": 315,
-                "weight": 0.32227
+                "weight": 0.42227</code></pre></figure>
<figure><figcaption><span class="label fail">2 · The refusal</span> named, with the value found</figcaption>
<pre><code>  <span class="v-fail">FAIL</span>  A20_MESH_WEIGHTS_COHERENT: mesh "neck"
        vertex 0 weights sum to 1.1000
        (see rigc guide A20_MESH_WEIGHTS_COHERENT)
  ..    52 assertions: 21 measured
        (20 passed, 1 failed), 17 skipped
rigc: 1 assertion(s) failed — nothing written
exit=1</code></pre></figure>
<figure><figcaption><span class="label pass">3 · After the fix</span> the same command, green</figcaption>
<pre><code>  ..    52 assertions: 21 measured
        (21 passed, 0 failed), 17 skipped,
        14 not in profile "spine"
rigc: wrote build/skeleton.json
rigc: wrote build/skeleton.atlas
rigc: wrote build/skeleton.model.json
exit=0</code></pre></figure>
</div>

<p class="mod-skip">Real output from Character 1's rig, <code>rig-c</code> 2.61.0 (long lines wrapped). Why the summary says 52 when the gate has 50 rules: <a href="#how-the-gate-decides">below</a>. Skip to <a href="#install">Install</a> · <a href="#inputs-and-outputs">Inputs and outputs</a> · <a href="#limits">Limits</a> · <a href="#go-deeper">Docs</a></p>

*This page follows Character 1 from the Family set: here it is checked. Every module works on its own; this order is one path, not a requirement.*

An agent authoring a rig cannot tell whether it succeeded, because Spine's JSON parser accepts a lot of nonsense silently: a constraint in the 4.2 shape simply vanishes, a `size:` that disagrees with the PNG collapses every UV, a four-number curve array yields NaN. Each of these loads clean, plays, and is wrong. `rigc` makes the failure legible: every refusal names its rule and the value it found, ends with the command that explains it, and leaves nothing on disk.

<figure class="figure-media">
  <div class="media">
    <video data-loop="the key-pose film" controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" poster="/assets/docs/core-keypose-poster.jpg" width="600" height="404" aria-label="Recorded video: two key poses of a drawn character side by side, rigc pose's report on where each part sits, two candidate in-between motions playing side by side, a rigc vote ballot with B chosen, and the chosen motion at full size — core's own film two">
      <source src="/assets/docs/core-keypose.mp4" type="video/mp4">
      <img src="/assets/docs/core-keypose-poster.jpg" alt="Two key poses of a drawn character side by side, with the command under them" width="600" height="404">
    </video>
  </div>
  <figcaption><span class="media-kind">Recorded video</span> rig-c core's own film two, the authoring loop on one character. Two key poses are the given conditions; <code>rigc pose</code> reads back where every part sits in each picture; two candidate in-betweenings are compiled from the same pair; and a real <code>rigc vote</code> ballot picks the winner — the movement between the poses is the one thing nothing in the toolchain grades. Five shots: the two pictures, <code>rigc pose</code>'s report on pose B, the two candidates, a photograph of the real ballot page, and the winner at full size; the command in the band is the one that produced the shot above it. Everything on screen is compiled output or a photograph of a real page, and every number on it was printed first by a tool. The character is film one's; the poses and the three motion specs are the only new authoring. From the <a href="https://github.com/rig-c/core">rig-c/core</a> README, built under the package's earlier name, <code>spine-rigc</code> — shot 2 is spine-rigc 0.9.0's report, not what <code>rigc pose</code> prints today.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Three mistakes an agent makes, on one rig

Each case starts from a fresh copy of Character 1's `rig.json`, `motion.json` and its 17 part images, built with `bunx rig-c@2.61.0 build --rig rig.json --motion motion.json --images images --out build`.

<div class="case">

### <span class="label fail">compile</span> A slot names a bone that does not exist

```diff
     {
       "name": "face",
-      "bone": "head",
+      "bone": "haed",
       "attachment": "face"
```

```
rigc compile error: rig.json: slot "face" names bone "haed", which this rig does not declare (see rigc guide CE_RIG_SLOT_BONE_UNKNOWN)
exit=1
```

`rigc guide CE_RIG_SLOT_BONE_UNKNOWN` prints that rule's row from the authoring guide, fix included: *Name a declared bone in slot.bone.* No `build/` directory exists afterwards.

</div>

<div class="case">

### <span class="label fail">compile</span> An image the rig names was renamed on disk

`mv images/hair_front.png images/hair-front.png`, with `rig.json` still naming `hair_front.png`:

```
rigc compile error: image "hair_front.png" is not on disk at images/hair_front.png (see rigc guide CE_COMPILE_IMAGE_MISSING)
exit=1
```

The guide's fix: *Supply the PNG at the named images path or correct the image name.*

</div>

<div class="case">

### <span class="label fail">gate</span> One vertex's weights do not sum to 1

This one compiles; the gate measures it and refuses — the case at the top of this page. Its guide row covers *a weighted vertex with no bone, a negative weight, a bone index out of range, or weights that do not sum to 1*.

</div>

Put each value back and the same command passes, writing files byte-identical to the clean build. The two compile refusals stop before the gate runs, so they print no assertion summary; the third is a gate `FAIL` with one.

## Passing is structural; looking is separate

A green gate says the data is valid Spine 4.3 that plays without errors — in core's own words, *a rig with its head off its torso passes the gate*. So rigc also draws what it built, with no reference needed:

<div class="compare">
  <figure><img src="/assets/docs/core-render-contact.jpg" alt="A contact sheet of Character 1's idle: 41 small frames of the full figure" width="401" height="775" loading="lazy"><figcaption><code>rigc render --candidate build --animation idle</code> — <code>idle 41 frame(s), 3.333s + contact.png</code></figcaption></figure>
  <figure><img src="/assets/docs/core-inspect-weights.jpg" alt="The neck mesh over dimmed art, coloured by how much each vertex follows the chest bone: blue near the head, red near the chest, with the triangle edges drawn" width="443" height="512" loading="lazy"><figcaption><code>rigc inspect … --show art,weights:chest,mesh --zoom slot:neck</code> — the neck mesh after the fix, coloured by its chest weight</figcaption></figure>
</div>

When a person needs to judge the motion against footage and hand back notes, that is [Review](/docs/review/).

## How the gate decides

1. **Measure the art.** rigc reads the PNGs themselves instead of trusting sizes you typed, so the skeleton and the atlas cannot drift apart.
2. **Compile two specs.** The rig spec (`rigc-rig/1`) holds structure — bones, slots in draw order, skins. The motion spec (`rigc-motion/1`) holds time — animations, tracks, keys.
3. **Gate.** The default profile, `spine`, runs the 36 validity rules: *is this valid Spine 4.3 that any runtime plays correctly?* `--profile rig-play` runs all 50; the extra 14 are one renderer's and one canvas budget's policy, which is why they are opt-in. Every report names its profile and lists, on `PROF` lines, the rules it left out.

   **Why a report counts 52.** The registry holds 50 named assertions, and `spine` + the 14 policy rules = 50. The published package links no Spine runtime, so the round trip's own parse, `A00_ROUNDTRIP_PARSE`, reports SKIP; in its place the report also carries the model side's two parse rules, `A00_MODEL_READ` and `A00_MODEL_REGIONS_ON_PAGES`, which the registry does not hold — so the summary totals 52 (rig-c 2.61.0, as in the runs on this page: 21 measured + 17 skipped + 14 not in profile `spine`).
4. **Write, or refuse.** Only a green gate writes `--out`.

The published package links no Spine runtime, so `A00_ROUNDTRIP_PARSE` — Spine's own parse — reports SKIP. Install `@esotericsoftware/spine-core` beside it and the same `rigc` runs that round trip too, plus `validate`, `preview`, `vote`, `bench` and `bonedist`.

**Key terms.** *Rig spec* — bones, the slots array (the setup draw order) and skins. *Motion spec* — the time file, aimed at the rig by name. *Named assertion* — a rule the gate runs; each failure names it. *Profile* — the rulebook: `spine` (default) or `rig-play`. *`ingest`* — `build` run backwards: a Spine 4.3 `skeleton.json` in, the two specs that rebuild it byte for byte out.

## Install

```sh
bun add -d rig-c
bun rigc build --rig rig.json --motion motion.json --out build/
```

rigc runs on Bun 1.2.0 or later. The npm package is `rig-c`; `@rig-c/core` is the same package under the scope, and the command is `rigc`. Licensing by playback path: [Licensing](/docs/licensing/).

## Inputs and outputs

| In | Out |
| --- | --- |
| Part PNGs | `skeleton.json` + `skeleton.atlas` — Spine 4.3 data |
| A rig spec (`rig.json`) | `skeleton.model.json` — rig-c's own compiled model, for [Play](/docs/play/) |
| A motion spec (`motion.json`) | the gate report (`--report` also writes it as JSON) |
| — | on a refusal: the named lines, and nothing on disk |

## Limits

- **The gate is structural.** It does not judge the picture; `render` and `inspect` are for looking.
- **The round trip needs spine-core.** Without it, `A00_ROUNDTRIP_PARSE` is SKIP and `validate`, `preview`, `vote`, `bench`, `bonedist` do not run.
- **Packing is opt-in and narrow** — `--pack` and `--atlas-in` do no trimming, rotation or scaling.
- **It emits Spine's format.** What a product may do with that data, and with a Spine Runtime, is in [Licensing](/docs/licensing/).

# @rig-c/review

<p class="mod-role">A local inspection page for a person: open what an agent built, find what looks wrong, pin it to a frame and a slot, and hand it back as an issue.</p>

<figure class="mod-hero">
  <img src="/assets/docs/review-screen.jpg" alt="The rig-review page: the left column lists checkpoints and source files, the centre shows Character 1's shirt part zoomed in with a dashed selection box, the right column lists all 17 slots with topwear selected, and the Feedback panel below shows one saved defect on slot topwear" width="1600" height="1000">
  <figcaption>Character 1's build from before the shoulder repair, open in <code>rig-review</code> 0.2.1: <code>topwear</code> soloed and zoomed, one defect saved against it, the review submitted as <em>changes requested</em>.</figcaption>
</figure>

<p class="mod-skip">Skip to <a href="#install">Install</a> · <a href="#inputs-and-outputs">Inputs and outputs</a> · <a href="#limits">Limits</a> · <a href="#go-deeper">Docs</a></p>

*This page follows Character 1 from the Family set: here it is looked at. Every module works on its own; this order is one path, not a requirement.*

The checks that keep a broken rig off the disk are structural: a shoulder that renders flat passes all of them. Someone has to look — and what they find has to reach whoever fixes it as something more precise than a screenshot. Review runs on your machine (`127.0.0.1` only), plays the build with the same `@rig-c/play` runtime a site would use, and records feedback bound to a frame range, a slot or bone, and the exact camera, without touching the files it was given.

## One problem, from seeing it to the fix

Character 1's shirt once had a flat, indented shoulder: an earlier preparation script had cut away cloth that the hair covers in the still and uncovers when it moves. The family suite records that repair in [its shoulder-repair note](https://github.com/rig-c/parts-examples/blob/main/family/roa/SHOULDER_REPAIR.md). Here it is replayed in Review on the build from before the repair.

<figure class="figure-media">
  <div class="media">
    <video data-loop="the review flow" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" poster="/assets/docs/review-flow-poster.jpg" width="1200" height="750" aria-label="Recorded video: the rig-review page with Character 1's build; the idle is paused at 1.25 seconds, the topwear slot is picked, soloed and zoomed until the step in the screen-left shoulder shows, the slot is used for feedback with frames 15 to 15, category Defect and a one-line summary, the feedback is added and the review submitted as changes requested, and the exported feedback JSON is shown">
      <source src="/assets/docs/review-flow.mp4" type="video/mp4">
      <img src="/assets/docs/review-flow-poster.jpg" alt="The rig-review page with Character 1's whole rig playing its idle" width="1200" height="750">
    </video>
  </div>
  <figcaption><span class="media-kind">Recorded video</span> The whole case in 15 seconds: <code>rig-review</code> 0.2.1 driven through its own page on Character 1's check build at parts-examples <code>144f556</code>, before the repair — pause at 1.25 s, pick and solo <code>topwear</code>, zoom on the shoulder, pin it as feedback, submit, export. Nothing is edited but the cut at both ends; the cursor is drawn in, and the last shot is the downloaded JSON opened in the same browser.</figcaption>
</figure>

<div class="case">

### 1. Open the build, and look where the motion would reveal it

`rig-review open <dir>` checks the folder and prints a loopback URL. In the whole rig the back hair covers the spot, so the reviewer pauses the idle, picks `topwear` in the parts list, ticks *Solo selected slot* and zooms in.

<figure class="figure-wide">
  <img src="/assets/docs/review-in-context.jpg" alt="The whole rig at the same zoom: the back hair covers the shoulder" width="1200" height="750" loading="lazy">
  <figcaption>The same camera with every slot drawn — the hair hides what the solo view shows.</figcaption>
</figure>

</div>

<div class="case">

### 2. Pin it, and submit

*Use slot for feedback*, then a category, a frame range and one line of summary; *Submit review* with status *Changes requested*. The export is plain JSON (or issue-ready Markdown):

```json
{
  "schema": "rig-review-feedback/1",
  "reviewedSource": {
    "viewerVersion": "0.2.1", "runtimeVersion": "1.12.0",
    "rig": { "path": "build/skeleton.model.json", "sha256": "28490ee9e2c7fa8a…" }
  },
  "status": "changes-requested",
  "feedback": [{
    "frameStart": 15, "frameEnd": 15,
    "target": { "kind": "slot", "name": "topwear" },
    "category": "defect",
    "summary": "Screen-left shoulder top of topwear is flat and indented (cloth alpha cut); exposed when hair moves aside",
    "context": { "animation": "idle", "time": 1.25, "frame": null,
                 "camera": { "zoom": 7.3586, "x": -112.72, "y": 1792.86, "coordinateSystem": "world-y-up" } }
  }]
}
```

The rig's hash, the viewer and runtime versions and the saved camera mean anyone holding the issue can reopen exactly this view. `"frame": null` is honest: this build declares no frame clock, so Review shows `rate unknown`, and the 15 is a number the reviewer entered (1.25 s at the check sampler's 12 fps).

</div>

<div class="case">

### 3. The fix happens upstream; the rebuilt rig comes back

Review changes nothing in the package — the repair was made in the authoring workflow: a guarded stage restored the original shirt cloth in that area and widened five outline vertices, then the rig was rebuilt and checked through the ordinary gates. Reopened in Review with the same view:

<figure class="figure-wide">
  <img src="/assets/docs/review-before-after.jpg" alt="Two close-ups of the shoulder: left, flat with a step; right, a smooth rounded shoulder" width="1296" height="400" loading="lazy">
  <figcaption>Left: before the repair, as pinned. Right: the current build, same time, slot and camera.</figcaption>
</figure>

</div>

Review also lines a build up against reference footage — side by side, synchronized cameras, frame strips — which is how a retargeted motion like the [Pose](/docs/pose/) page's cup swing gets judged against what it was meant to copy.

## Install
```sh
npm i -D @rig-c/review
npx rig-review open /absolute/path/to/output
```
Runs under Bun 1.3.0 or later, which must be on `PATH`; `open` prints a loopback URL and exits (README §"Start").

## Inputs and outputs
| In | Out |
| --- | --- |
| An output folder: `skeleton.model.json` (root or `build/`), `motion.json`, `report.json`, `skeleton.json`/`.skel`/`.atlas` | A loopback inspection page (`127.0.0.1` only) |
| Source references: videos (`.mp4`, `.webm`, `.mov`), strip/contact/sheet images, `*pose*.json` sequences | Saved review session: status, checkpoint outcomes and feedback, under `~/.local/state/rig-c-review/` |
| (optional) a curated `review.json` with checkpoints, references and angle axes | Feedback export as JSON or issue-ready Markdown (`feedback --format issue`) |
| For `compare`: two outputs and one local reference video | Frame strips as PNG (plus a `.png.json` provenance sidecar) or JSON |

## Limits
- **"Motion is view, annotate and export only."** It never retimes, authors keys, or writes `motion.json` (README, intro).
- **No modeling touch-up yet**: it "does not edit meshes, weights or source art" (README, intro).
- **`check` validates the delivery contract and model envelope**, not the upstream compiler gate or visual quality; a raw `skeleton.json` can be inspected but not played (README §"Existing output handoff").
- **No frame rate is inferred**: without a declared clock the page shows `rate unknown`, and strip PNGs need the report's exact `frameTimes` (README §"Existing output handoff", §"Frame strip export").
- **Never publishes an issue automatically**; saving or exporting feedback modifies no model (README §"Feedback ownership").
- **Maturity**: "the CLI is the supported surface, and no importable API is promised yet" (README §"Start"; the README still says 0.1.x while npm is at 0.2.1).

- [docs/DESIGN.md](https://github.com/rig-c/review/blob/main/docs/DESIGN.md) — the runnable foundation vs. future modeling touch-up

# @rig-c/play

<p class="mod-role">The browser player for the model rigc writes — no Spine runtime, rigid parts as plain DOM elements or the whole rig in one canvas.</p>

The live player on this page plays Character 1 with two motions (idle and the cup swing from the Pose page), with play/pause, DOM or canvas mode, and bone and mesh overlays. It needs JavaScript.

<p class="mod-skip">Skip to <a href="#a-minimal-page">A minimal page</a> · <a href="#install">Install</a> · <a href="#inputs-and-outputs">Inputs and outputs</a> · <a href="#limits">Limits</a> · <a href="#go-deeper">Docs</a></p>

*This page follows Character 1 from the Family set: here it is played. Every module works on its own; this order is one path, not a requirement.*

A rigged character usually means a canvas runtime that rasterizes everything. For a rigid part, though, the bone transform is a plain affine map that CSS `matrix()` expresses exactly — so the rigid parts can live in the DOM, where the browser composites them and you can inspect and style them like any element. Play keeps that path, and adds what the DOM cannot do alone: per-part mesh canvases, `clip-path` clipping, and skipping meshes that did not move. Switch the player above to **One canvas** to see the other mode draw the same pose.

## What you just ran

The player above is the published package doing what any page does with it — nothing on this site poses the rig:

1. `loadModel()` read Character 1's `skeleton.model.json` and cut each atlas region into its own bitmap (the `.atlas` and `skeleton.json` beside it are not fetched).
2. `new RigPlayer(root, assets, { mode })` opened the motion you picked on a live track; rig-c's core, bundled in the package, poses bones, constraints, physics and draw order on the CPU, one `frame(dt)` at a time.
3. Each frame became a `PosedFrame` — region corners or mesh vertices, UVs, tint and clip, in draw order. A region is written as one `matrix()` string; meshes draw through one shared WebGL context and fall back to canvas2d (the status line says which ran).
4. **Bones** and **Mesh** draw from the player's own read-only queries, `bone(name)` and `posedFrame()`; **Pause** calls `pause()`.

`swing` — the cup swung like a pendulum — is the motion the [Pose](/docs/pose/) page retargeted onto this rig; `idle` came with the rig from [Parts](/docs/parts/).

## A minimal page

Twenty-odd lines, from the README, load a model from jsDelivr, fit its stage box to a container and drive the clock:

```html
<div id="stage" style="position: relative; width: 480px; height: 640px; overflow: hidden"></div>
<script type="module">
  import { loadModel, RigPlayer } from 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@rig-c/play@1/dist/index.js';
  const stage = document.getElementById('stage');
  const assets = await loadModel({ modelUrl: 'rigs/look/skeleton.model.json' });
  const root = stage.appendChild(document.createElement('div'));
  const player = new RigPlayer(root, assets);
  player.play(assets.animations[0].name);
  const box = assets.stage ?? player.bounds();
  const scale = Math.min(stage.clientWidth / box.width, stage.clientHeight / box.height);
  root.style.cssText = `position: absolute; transform-origin: 0 0; transform: scale(${scale});
    left: ${-box.x * scale}px; top: ${(box.y + box.height) * scale}px`;
  player.renderer.syncPixelRatio();
  let last = performance.now();
  requestAnimationFrame(function tick(now) {
    player.frame((now - last) / 1000);
    last = now;
    requestAnimationFrame(tick);
  });
</script>
```

The player does not run its own clock: the page calls `frame(dt)`, so pausing, slowing down or stopping the loop is yours to decide (this site's player stays paused when your system asks for reduced motion). To play the same model inside PixiJS, Phaser or Three.js, see the [adapters](/docs/adapters/).

**Key terms.** *Model document* — `skeleton.model.json` (spec `rigc-compiled/3`). *Region attachment* — a rigid part, an `<img>` with a CSS matrix. *Mesh attachment* — a deforming part on its own small canvas. *Render mode* — `dom` (default) or `canvas`. *Mesh backend* — `webgl` (default since 1.9) or `canvas2d`. *Attachment set* — a named swap of slot attachments from `sets.json`.

## Install

```sh
npm i @rig-c/play
npm i -D rig-c    # rigc build writes the model the player loads
```

Runs in the browser as an ES module; rig-c's posing core is bundled, so there is nothing else to install. The package is MIT and links nothing from Esoteric Software — see [Licensing](/docs/licensing/).

## Inputs and outputs
| In | Out |
| --- | --- |
| `skeleton.model.json` — the compiled model `rigc build` writes (spec `rigc-compiled/3`) | DOM mode (default): one `<img>` per rigid slot posed by a CSS `matrix()`, small per-part canvases for meshes |
| Its atlas page images (the `.atlas` and `skeleton.json` beside it are not fetched) | Canvas mode: the whole frame in one `<canvas>` per player |
| (optional) `sets.json` — named attachment sets, spec `rig-parts-sets/1` | Reads off the pose: `player.bone(name)`, `player.bounds()`, `slotIdentity()` |
| (optional) your own `PosedFrame` records, via `DomRenderer.render` | |

## Limits
From the README's *Status* and *No counterpart in 1.0.0* (it has no limits section):
- **Status: "Production."** — 60 fps on every engine measured for the practical scenario (README §"Status").
- **Reads rigc's model only**: "a Spine export is refused by name"; `loadModel` reads a compiled model document and nothing else (README §"Why", §"No counterpart in 1.0.0").
- **Which render mode is faster where is "not measured on a device yet"**, so the default stays `dom` (README §"Status").
- **Dark/two-colour tint stays out of scope in DOM mode**; RGB tint needs reference-filter support, Safari 15+ (README §"Status").
- **Clipping caveats**: an inverse polygon matches Spine's clipper only when convex, and the cost of many `clip-path`s on real-device Safari is not measured (README §"Status").
- **No per-slot changes from code** (attachment, colour) and no `scale` on load; scaling the root element is the caller's (README §"No counterpart in 1.0.0").

- [Attachment sets (`sets.json`)](https://github.com/rig-c/play#attachment-sets-setsjson)
- [Runtime knobs and what they cost](https://github.com/rig-c/play#runtime-knobs-and-what-they-cost)

# Engine adapters

The adapters put a rigc-built rig inside the engine or renderer your game already uses. [Play](/docs/play/) computes the pose; the host draws it with its own objects.

## What it is

Three packages, each versioned on its own, all at 0.1.1 with 0.x APIs:

- `@rig-c/pixi`: a PixiJS 8 adapter.
- `@rig-c/phaser`: a Phaser 4.2+ adapter for WebGL scenes.
- `@rig-c/three`: a native Three.js 0.186.1 renderer and live `Group`.

Each one reads the model document `rigc build` writes, `skeleton.model.json`, through `@rig-c/play`.

<figure class="figure-wide">
  <div class="media">
    <video data-loop="the walk" controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" poster="/assets/docs/adapters-three-engines-poster.jpg" width="1424" height="638" aria-label="Recorded video: the same cartoon animal character walking in place in three panels, labelled PixiJS, Phaser and Three.js, in step with each other">
      <source src="/assets/docs/adapters-three-engines.mp4" type="video/mp4">
      <img src="/assets/docs/adapters-three-engines-poster.jpg" alt="The same walking character in three panels labelled @rig-c/pixi, @rig-c/phaser and @rig-c/three" width="1424" height="638">
    </video>
  </div>
  <figcaption><span class="media-kind">Recorded video</span> One rig, three hosts: <code>@rig-c/pixi</code> 0.1.1 on PixiJS 8.22.0, <code>@rig-c/phaser</code> 0.1.1 on Phaser 4.2.1 and <code>@rig-c/three</code> 0.1.1 on Three.js 0.186.1. Each panel is the adapters repository's own demo page, run against the npm releases, playing rigc's <code>walk</code> gallery rig and its 0.9 s <code>walk</code> animation; all three read the same <code>skeleton.model.json</code> through <code>@rig-c/play</code> 1.10.0, unmodified. Every frame was posed by seeking each page to the same time (30 fps) and reading its WebGL canvas, and the 0.9 s cycle plays four times. At equal times the panels differ by a mean of 0.03 (PixiJS vs Phaser) and 0.54 (PixiJS vs Three.js) on 0–255 RGB, against 2.4 between neighbouring frames; the Three.js demo draws the rig smaller, so its panel is enlarged more.</figcaption>
</figure>

## When to use it

Use an adapter when your game or page already renders with PixiJS, Phaser or Three.js, and the rig must sit in that scene graph with your other objects. Three.js is a 3D renderer, so its adapter is for 2D characters inside 3D scenes and interactive pages.

If you only need a rig in a web page, with no engine, use [Play](/docs/play/) directly. It draws as DOM elements or one canvas. Native engines such as Godot or Unity are planned, not available.

## What it solves

rigc compiles a rig into two things side by side: Spine 4.3 skeleton data and its own model document. An official Spine runtime can load the Spine data, but it brings the Spine Runtimes licence with it. An adapter is a third way: rig-c's own poser runs inside the engine's scene graph and renderer, reads the model document, and links no Spine runtime.

## What you get

- **A live object** per host: `PixiRig` (a Pixi `Container`), `PhaserRig` (a Phaser `Container`) and `ThreeRig` (a flat Three.js `Group`). Each owns an independent player and exposes `play`, `seek`, `bone()` and `bounds()`.
- **A renderer** per host for when you own the player: `PixiRenderer`, `PhaserRenderer` and `ThreeRenderer`. Each draws a supplied `PosedFrame`.
- **Shared page textures**: several rigs over one `ModelAssets` load share page textures until the last holder releases them.

## How it works

1. Load the model with `@rig-c/play`'s `loadModel`, using the files `rigc build` wrote, unmodified.
2. Create the host object, for example `new PixiRig(assets, { ticker: app.ticker })`, and add it to your stage or scene.
3. Each update, `@rig-c/play` poses the rig and produces a `PosedFrame` record.
4. The adapter reads slot corners or mesh vertices, page UVs, tint, blend and clip straight from that record. It maps world `(x, y)` to `(x, -y)` and draws with the host's native objects.
5. On removal, `destroy()` frees that rig's own resources. Dispose the shared assets after the last rig is gone.

```sh
npm install @rig-c/pixi pixi.js @rig-c/play
```

Swap in `@rig-c/phaser phaser` or `@rig-c/three three` for the other hosts.

## Key concepts

- **Host**: the engine or renderer an adapter targets. Each host lives in `packages/<host>`.
- **Model document**: `skeleton.model.json`, the source the adapters read. Spine is one export of it.
- **`PosedFrame`**: the per-frame record `@rig-c/play` produces and every renderer draws.
- **`ModelAssets`**: one `loadModel` result, which several rigs can share.
- **Parity**: an adapter plays the same pose for the same time as `@rig-c/play`, held to the player's output by a test.

## Go deeper

- [README: Why this exists](https://github.com/rig-c/adapters#why-this-exists)

# Licensing

Three separate questions, answered separately: the licence of rig-c's own code, the Spine terms that come with the way you play the output, and the licence of the sample paintings and layers. This page restates rig-c's notices and Esoteric Software's published terms; it is not legal advice, and the originals linked below are what count.

## rig-c's own code: MIT

`rig-c` (core), `@rig-c/parts`, `@rig-c/pose`, `@rig-c/review`, `@rig-c/play`, `@rig-c/pixi`, `@rig-c/phaser` and `@rig-c/three` are MIT — each repository's `LICENSE`. That grant covers rig-c's code. It says nothing about Spine, and it does not cover the sample assets below.

## Spine terms: they follow what plays the output

`rigc build` writes two things side by side: **Spine 4.3 skeleton data** (`skeleton.json` + `skeleton.atlas`) and **rig-c's own model** (`skeleton.model.json`). rig-c core's [NOTICE](https://github.com/rig-c/core/blob/main/NOTICE.md) puts the rule in one line: *what the terms turn on is the integration* of a Spine Runtime — and rigc *neither adds those terms nor removes them*.

| Path | What plays or opens the output | Terms that apply |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rig-c's model in a page or an engine | [`@rig-c/play`](/docs/play/), [`@rig-c/pixi` / `phaser` / `three`](/docs/adapters/) | rig-c's MIT. These packages link nothing from Esoteric Software and pose the rig with rig-c's own core, so no Spine Runtime is integrated. |
| Spine data in a product | an official Spine Runtime, or the Spine Web Player (which `rigc preview` loads) | The [Spine Runtimes License](https://esotericsoftware.com/spine-runtimes-license): integration is permitted under Section 2 of the Spine Editor License Agreement, or on the condition that each user of the product obtains their own Spine Editor licence, and redistribution includes that licence and copyright notice. |
| Spine data in the Spine editor | the Spine editor, to refine by hand | The [Spine Editor License Agreement](https://esotericsoftware.com/spine-editor-license). |
| rigc with `@esotericsoftware/spine-core` installed beside it | rigc's round-trip gate, `validate`, `preview`, `vote`, `bench`, `bonedist` | That install integrates a Spine Runtime, so the Spine Runtimes License applies there. The published `rig-c` package does not carry spine-core. |

Esoteric Software's licence pages read *Last updated April 5, 2025* when this page was written.

## Sample assets carry their own licences

| Assets | Licence | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The painting and layers [Getting started](/docs/getting-started/) downloads | **CC BY-NC 4.0** — credit required, no commercial use; what you build from them carries that licence | [rig-c/exam `LICENSE`](https://github.com/rig-c/exam/blob/main/LICENSE) |
| The paintings, See-through inputs and layers in [rig-c/parts-examples](https://github.com/rig-c/parts-examples) | MIT | [`LICENSE`](https://github.com/rig-c/parts-examples/blob/main/LICENSE) |
| The trailer's painting, layers, sky, palm and rendered trailer | MIT | [rig-c/trailer `LICENSE`](https://github.com/rig-c/trailer/blob/main/LICENSE) |

The image models that generated those paintings, and See-through itself, have their own terms; each repository's `NOTICE.md` records them, and [rig-c/parts `NOTICE.md`](https://github.com/rig-c/parts/blob/main/NOTICE.md) collects See-through's. No rig-c package contains See-through code or weights.
